ideas.title: Identity Over Outcome
ideas.body: Lasting change starts with who you decide to become, not the result you're chasing. Every small habit is a vote for a certain kind of person.

ideas.title: The Four Laws
ideas.body: Make cues obvious, cravings attractive, actions easy, and rewards satisfying. Reverse each law to break a habit instead of building one.

ideas.title: 1% Better
ideas.body: Tiny, consistent improvements compound over months into results that feel sudden but were actually earned daily.

ideas.title: Environment Design
ideas.body: Willpower is overrated. Shape your surroundings so the good choice becomes the easy, obvious one.

ideas.title: Never Miss Twice
ideas.body: One slip is an accident. Two in a row is the start of a new habit — get back on track immediately.

ideas.title: Shared Fictions
ideas.body: Humans lead the planet because we believe in things that exist only in imagination — money, nations, laws — and cooperate at scale because of it.

ideas.title: The Cognitive Revolution
ideas.body: A rewiring of the human mind gave us flexible language, letting rumors, myths, and plans spread across entire tribes.

ideas.title: The Agricultural Trap
ideas.body: Farming didn't liberate humanity — it tied people to land and often meant harder lives for the many, surplus for the few.

ideas.title: Money as Trust
ideas.body: Currency is the most universal story ever told — a system of mutual trust that lets total strangers cooperate.

ideas.title: The Unhappiness Question
ideas.body: Progress in power hasn't guaranteed progress in wellbeing. History's biggest gains didn't always make individual lives better.

ideas.title: The Deep Work Hypothesis
ideas.body: The ability to focus without distraction is becoming rare and valuable — those who cultivate it will thrive.

ideas.title: Attention Residue
ideas.body: Switching tasks leaves mental residue that drags down performance on whatever comes next. Batching beats multitasking.

ideas.title: Rituals Over Willpower
ideas.body: Fixed routines around when and where you do deep work remove decision fatigue and make focus automatic.

ideas.title: Embrace Boredom
ideas.body: Constant stimulation trains your brain to crave distraction. Practicing stillness rebuilds your capacity to concentrate.

ideas.title: Judge Your Tools
ideas.body: Evaluate apps and platforms by whether they serve your core goals, not by the fear of missing out.

ideas.title: Two Systems
ideas.body: System 1 is fast, intuitive, emotional. System 2 is slow and deliberate. Most of daily life runs on System 1 — for better and worse.

ideas.title: Anchoring
ideas.body: An early number, even an irrelevant one, quietly shapes every estimate that follows it.

ideas.title: Loss Aversion
ideas.body: Losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains feel good, which explains why people avoid reasonable risks.

ideas.title: The Availability Heuristic
ideas.body: We judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind, not by actual frequency.

ideas.title: Planning Fallacy
ideas.body: We reliably underestimate how long tasks will take, even when we know the pattern from experience.

ideas.title: Seek Wealth, Not Money
ideas.body: Wealth is owning assets that earn while you sleep. Money is just a social IOU for time and value.

ideas.title: Specific Knowledge
ideas.body: Skills built through genuine curiosity can't be trained by anyone else — no one can outsource or automate them.

ideas.title: Play Long-Term Games
ideas.body: Compounding, in relationships, knowledge, and money, rewards the people who simply stay in the game longest.

ideas.title: Judgment Over Effort
ideas.body: In an age of leverage, good judgment matters more than hours worked. Think clearly before acting quickly.

ideas.title: Happiness Is a Skill
ideas.body: Peace comes from wanting what you already have — practiced deliberately, like any other skill.

ideas.title: The Last Freedom
ideas.body: Everything can be taken from a person except the choice of how to respond to what happens. That gap between event and reaction is where a life is decided.

ideas.title: Meaning Over Happiness
ideas.body: Happiness can't be pursued directly; it follows from having a reason to act. Chase the reason and the feeling arrives on its own.

ideas.title: Three Roads to Meaning
ideas.body: Meaning comes from work worth doing, from love for someone, or from the courage found in unavoidable suffering. Most lives use all three.

ideas.title: Suffering With Purpose
ideas.body: Pain that means something is bearable in a way pointless pain never is. Naming the purpose changes what a person can carry.

ideas.title: The Why Carries the How
ideas.body: Someone with a reason to live can survive almost any circumstance. Without one, comfort alone won't hold a person together.

ideas.title: Fixed and Growth
ideas.body: A fixed mindset treats ability as a fact to be defended. A growth mindset treats it as something that changes with effort.

ideas.title: Praise the Process
ideas.body: Telling someone they're smart makes them protect the label. Praising how they worked makes them willing to try something harder.

ideas.title: Failure as Information
ideas.body: To a fixed mindset a setback is a verdict. To a growth mindset it's data about what to practise next.

ideas.title: The Power of Yet
ideas.body: "I can't do this" and "I can't do this yet" describe the same moment and lead to entirely different next weeks.

ideas.title: Mindsets Are Situational
ideas.body: Nobody holds one mindset everywhere. You can be growth-minded at work and quietly fixed about the thing you keep avoiding.

ideas.title: Nobody's Crazy
ideas.body: Everyone's financial decisions make sense given what they've lived through. Your caution and their risk-taking were both taught by experience.

ideas.title: Enough
ideas.body: The hardest financial skill is knowing when to stop. Without a definition of enough, more money keeps moving the finish line.

ideas.title: Room for Error
ideas.body: The point of a margin of safety is to survive being wrong, because staying in the game is what compounding actually requires.

ideas.title: Wealth Is Invisible
ideas.body: Spending shows what someone bought. Wealth is what they didn't spend — and it's the part that buys freedom.

ideas.title: Tails Drive Everything
ideas.body: A small number of decisions produce most of the result. The rest of the work is patience while those few play out.

ideas.title: Vertical Progress
ideas.body: Copying what works takes the world from one to many. Building something that didn't exist takes it from zero to one.

ideas.title: Competition Is Overrated
ideas.body: Fierce competition destroys the profit it fights over. Valuable companies escape competition rather than win it.

ideas.title: The Secret Question
ideas.body: Every great business rests on a truth few people agree with. Ask what important thing you believe that almost nobody else does.

ideas.title: Start Small, Then Widen
ideas.body: Dominate a market small enough to own completely, then expand outward from a position nobody can easily attack.

ideas.title: The Last Mover
ideas.body: Being first matters far less than being the last company to make a large improvement in a market.

ideas.title: What Is Up to You
ideas.body: Judgement, effort, and response are yours. Reputation, outcomes, and other people are not. Confusing the two causes most unhappiness.

ideas.title: The Obstacle Becomes the Path
ideas.body: What blocks the action becomes the action. An impediment to a plan can be turned into the material of it.

ideas.title: Nothing Is New
ideas.body: Everything happening now has happened before to someone else. The situation is rarely as unprecedented as it feels.

ideas.title: The Work in Front of You
ideas.body: Do this task, well, as if it were the last thing you'll do. Most anxiety is about work that isn't yet at hand.

ideas.title: Remember the Ending
ideas.body: Keeping the finite in view isn't morbid. It's the fastest way to see what actually deserves an afternoon.

ideas.title: Tactical Empathy
ideas.body: Understanding the other side well enough to say their position out loud isn't agreement. It's leverage.

ideas.title: Labels and Mirrors
ideas.body: Saying "it seems like…", or simply repeating their last few words, invites people to keep explaining themselves.

ideas.title: No Is the Start
ideas.body: "No" makes people feel safe and in control. It's where a real conversation begins, not where it ends.

ideas.title: That's Right
ideas.body: Aim for the moment they say "that's right". It means you've summarised their view better than they did.

ideas.title: Calibrated Questions
ideas.body: "How am I supposed to do that?" hands the problem back without confrontation, and often produces their own concession.

ideas.title: The Extrovert Ideal
ideas.body: Modern workplaces were built on the assumption that talking is thinking, which quietly wastes half the room.

ideas.title: Solitude Matters
ideas.body: Deliberate practice is almost always solitary. Constant collaboration crowds out the conditions that produce good work.

ideas.title: The Brainstorming Problem
ideas.body: Groups brainstorming together generate fewer and weaker ideas than the same people working alone and pooling results afterwards.

ideas.title: Restorative Niches
ideas.body: Introverts can act extroverted for work they care about, as long as they get the quiet that pays the energy back.

ideas.title: Sensitivity as Signal
ideas.body: Reacting strongly to stimulation isn't weakness. It usually travels with noticing detail and consequences that others miss.

ideas.title: Less but Better
ideas.body: The essentialist doesn't ask how to fit everything in. They ask which few things are worth doing at all.

ideas.title: The Power of Choice
ideas.body: Saying yes to everything is a decision to let other people set your priorities for you.

ideas.title: If It's Not a Clear Yes
ideas.body: When something is merely good, treat it as a no. Only an obvious yes has earned the space.

ideas.title: Protect the Asset
ideas.body: Sleep, health, and attention produce everything else. Trading them for output is a terrible exchange rate.

ideas.title: Design the Routine
ideas.body: Willpower is finite; routine isn't. Building the essential into the default removes the daily argument with yourself.

ideas.title: Sleep Is Not Optional
ideas.body: Every biological system measured so far works worse on short sleep. No function has been found that improves with less of it.

ideas.title: Two Kinds of Sleep
ideas.body: Deep sleep moves memory into long-term storage. REM makes connections between what's stored. A night needs both.

ideas.title: Rhythm and Pressure
ideas.body: Two systems set sleep: a body clock, and a chemical that builds while you're awake. Caffeine blocks the second, not the first.

ideas.title: Debt Isn't Repaid
ideas.body: Lost sleep can't be recovered with a long weekend. The brain has no mechanism for reclaiming the hours it missed.

ideas.title: The Invisible Decline
ideas.body: Reaction time, learning, and emotional control all degrade before anyone notices. Poor sleepers reliably rate their own performance as fine.

ideas.title: Effort Counts Twice
ideas.body: Talent turns effort into skill, then effort turns skill into achievement. Effort appears in the equation both times.

ideas.title: Passion Is Direction
ideas.body: Grit isn't intensity. It's the same direction held for years, with one top-level goal organising everything beneath it.

ideas.title: Deliberate Practice
ideas.body: Improvement comes from working at the edge of your ability with real feedback, not from repeating what you've already mastered.

ideas.title: Setbacks Are Temporary
ideas.body: Gritty people read a failure as specific and passing rather than permanent proof. That reading is learned, not inherited.

ideas.title: Culture Carries It
ideas.body: Persistence is contagious. Who you spend your weeks around does more for it than any amount of self-talk.

ideas.title: Kind and Wicked Worlds
ideas.body: Early specialisation wins in games with fixed rules. Most of life has unclear rules and slow feedback, where breadth wins.

ideas.title: The Sampling Period
ideas.body: People who try several fields before committing tend to match themselves better, and improve faster once they do.

ideas.title: Analogies Over Details
ideas.body: Experts solve unfamiliar problems by borrowing structure from unrelated fields. Breadth is what makes the borrowing possible.

ideas.title: Desirable Difficulties
ideas.body: Learning that feels slow and effortful sticks. Learning that feels smooth usually doesn't survive the week.

ideas.title: Drop Your Tools
ideas.body: Expertise turns into a liability when the situation changes and the familiar method is the thing you can't put down.

ideas.title: Build, Measure, Learn
ideas.body: Treat a company as a series of experiments. The unit of progress is validated learning, not features shipped.

ideas.title: Minimum Viable Product
ideas.body: Build the smallest thing that tests the riskiest assumption. Anything more is investment in an answer you don't have yet.

ideas.title: Vanity Metrics
ideas.body: Totals that only ever rise flatter the team. Useful metrics compare cohorts and can tell you that you were wrong.

ideas.title: Pivot or Persevere
ideas.body: Scheduled, honest reviews of whether the strategy is working prevent the slow drift that nobody has to take responsibility for.

ideas.title: Small Batches
ideas.body: Shipping in small pieces surfaces problems while they're still cheap. Large batches hide them until they're expensive.

ideas.title: Decisions Are Bets
ideas.body: Every choice is a bet on an uncertain future made with incomplete information. Certainty was never on the table.

ideas.title: Resulting
ideas.body: Judging a decision by how it turned out confuses luck with skill, and teaches the wrong lesson in both directions.

ideas.title: Skill and Luck
ideas.body: Ask how much of this outcome you actually controlled. The answer decides whether to repeat the process or change it.

ideas.title: Say the Odds
ideas.body: Replacing "I'm sure" with a percentage makes a belief updatable, and makes being wrong survivable.

ideas.title: A Truth-Seeking Group
ideas.body: Find people who reward accuracy over agreement. Most groups quietly pay you to keep the opinion you already have.

ideas.title: The Habit Loop
ideas.body: Cue, routine, reward. Every habit runs the same three-part loop, whether it's flossing or reaching for your phone.

ideas.title: Keep the Cue and Reward
ideas.body: Habits aren't erased, they're replaced. Hold the cue and the reward steady, and change only the routine in between.

ideas.title: Craving Does the Work
ideas.body: Once the brain expects a reward, the cue produces wanting. The wanting, not the reward, is what makes it automatic.

ideas.title: Keystone Habits
ideas.body: Some habits reorganise the ones around them. Regular exercise or a shared meal quietly moves several unrelated behaviours.

ideas.title: Belief Holds the Gap
ideas.body: Under stress the old routine returns unless the person believes change is possible — and belief is usually something a group supplies.

ideas.title: Nose Over Mouth
ideas.body: The nose filters, warms, and regulates air. Mouth breathing skips all of it, and costs more than most people expect.

ideas.title: Slower Is Better
ideas.body: Around six breaths a minute settles heart rate and blood pressure. Most people breathe two to three times that fast.

ideas.title: Less Air, Not More
ideas.body: Overbreathing strips carbon dioxide, which is what lets oxygen leave the blood. Breathing less can deliver more.

ideas.title: The Long Exhale
ideas.body: A slow exhale is the fastest lever on the nervous system, which is why a sigh works before any thought does.

ideas.title: Built by Habit
ideas.body: Soft diets and slumped posture narrow the airway over years. How you breathe is partly built by how you live.

books.title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
books.author: Dale Carnegie

ideas.title: Criticism Doesn't Land
ideas.body: People defend themselves rather than update. Almost nobody blames themselves for anything, however plainly it's pointed out.

ideas.title: The Deepest Craving
ideas.body: Everyone wants to feel important. Honest, specific appreciation is rare enough that people remember it for years.

ideas.title: Be Interested
ideas.body: The fastest route to being found interesting is being interested. Ask, then listen longer than is comfortable.

ideas.title: Let It Be Their Idea
ideas.body: People support what they helped build. Ask the questions that let the other person arrive at the conclusion.

ideas.title: Admit It First
ideas.body: Saying you were wrong, quickly and without hedging, ends the argument that criticism would have started.

ideas.title: Beyond Resilience
ideas.body: Fragile things break under stress, resilient things endure it, antifragile things improve because of it. Most thinking stops at the middle one.

ideas.title: Via Negativa
ideas.body: Improvement usually comes from removing — the wrong food, the wrong obligation, the wrong exposure — rather than from adding something new.

ideas.title: Skin in the Game
ideas.body: Advice from someone who doesn't carry the downside should be priced accordingly. Exposure is what makes an opinion honest.

ideas.title: The Barbell
ideas.body: Keep most of your position extremely safe and a small part extremely aggressive. Avoid the moderate middle that hides its risk.

ideas.title: Small Errors, Often
ideas.body: Systems that absorb frequent small failures rarely suffer one enormous one. Suppressing every wobble only stores the damage up.

ideas.title: Retrieval Beats Review
ideas.body: Testing yourself builds memory. Rereading builds only the feeling of knowing — the comfortable method is the weaker one.

ideas.title: Space It Out
ideas.body: Leaving enough time to half-forget makes the next recall harder, and harder recall is what makes it durable.

ideas.title: Interleave the Practice
ideas.body: Mixing problem types feels worse during the session and performs better when the problems arrive unsorted, which is how they arrive.

ideas.title: Struggle First
ideas.body: Attempting a problem before being taught the method improves what the teaching then has to stick to.

ideas.title: Fluency Is a Trap
ideas.body: Ease of reading gets mistaken for mastery. If the material feels effortless, you're probably not learning much from it.

ideas.title: The World Improved
ideas.body: Extreme poverty, child mortality, and illiteracy have all fallen dramatically, and almost nobody guesses this correctly.

ideas.title: Four Levels, Not Two
ideas.body: There is no developed and developing world. Most people live somewhere in the middle, on incomes that keep rising.

ideas.title: The Gap Instinct
ideas.body: We picture two camps with a gulf between them. Look at the actual distribution and the gulf usually isn't there.

ideas.title: The Negativity Instinct
ideas.body: Bad news travels and gradual improvement doesn't. Things can be bad and getting better at the same time.

ideas.title: Ask for the Numbers
ideas.body: Before reacting to a trend, ask for the figure, the comparison, and the time frame. Most alarm doesn't survive all three.

ideas.title: Nothing Is Original
ideas.body: Everything builds on what came before. The useful theft is of structure and method, never of surface.

ideas.title: Copy to Find Yourself
ideas.body: Imitation is how a voice starts. The gap between what you copied and what came out is the beginning of your own style.

ideas.title: Make What's Missing
ideas.body: Build the thing you'd want to read, watch, or use and can't find. It's the most reliable brief there is.

ideas.title: Keep Your Hands In It
ideas.body: Screens are good for editing and bad for making. Keeping something physical in the loop changes what gets made.

ideas.title: Boring Is Productive
ideas.body: A stable, unremarkable routine funds interesting work. Chaos is expensive and delivers less than it promises.
